India’s forex reserves hit all-time high of $729.3 billion after RBI’s steps to attract capital

Steps taken by  RBI in early June hel avert what could have been an unprecedented third year of a deficit in India’s broadest measure of money flowing in and out of the economy.

Bhaskar Dutta

28 August, 2026 09:09 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representational Image | The Reserve Bank of India headquarters in Mumbai. Photographer: Dhiraj Singh/Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

India’s foreign-exchange reserves climbed to a record high as dollar inflows surged after recent measures by the central bank to attract capital.

The Reserve Bank of India’s forex stockpile gained by $12.4 billion to an all-time high of $729.3 billion in the week of Aug. 21, according to data released by the central bank Friday. That surpasses the previous high of $728.5 billion in February.

Steps taken by the RBI in early June, including a special deposit program for overseas citizens, have garnered $72.8 billion of inflows through Aug. 21. That’s helped avert what could have been an unprecedented third year of a deficit in India’s broadest measure of money flowing in and out of the economy.

Show Full Article

The boost to reserves has given the central bank more  firepower  to support the rupee, which remains one of Asia’s worst-performing currencies. The unit has recovered about 1.7% from a record low hit in May, but continues to face pressure from elevated oil prices, given the nation’s heavy dependence on fuel imports.

While the dollar inflows cushion India’s external situation, attracting them is expensive as the RBI is bearing banks’ hedging costs under the diaspora deposits, enabling lenders to offer lucrative interest rates to overseas customers.

It is costlier for the central bank to do so now as US interest rates are at much higher levels than they were in 2013, the last time the RBI turned to overseas residents for such deposits.

“The mobilization under the ongoing RBI swap scheme highlights the acute limitations of relying on expensive debt-funded reserve mobilization to stabilize the rupee,” Dhananjay Sinha, head of research at Systematix Shares and Stocks Ltd., wrote in a note.

The central bank typically deploys dollars in assets whose returns are substantially lower than the expense incurred in raising money under the special program, he wrote, adding that the “carry cost” for the country could be around $5.7 billion annually.

Earlier this month, the RBI unexpectedly brought forward the closure of the diaspora deposit program, with Governor Sanjay Malhotra saying flows had been stronger than expected.

OpenAI knew its AI models were behaving unusually before they went rogue & hacked Hugging Face

The models also tried to erase or tamper with their own activity logs to make it look as though they had not cheated on their assigned tasks, says Open AI report.

Vrinda Tulsian

28 August, 2026 06:08 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

The OpenAI logo | Reuters File Photo

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: OpenAI’s staff noticed unusual behaviour from its AI models, weeks before the models escaped a test system and hacked a widely used AI platform. However, the company decided not to stop the test, according to a report it has now published.

The models also tried to erase or tamper with their own activity logs to make it look as though they had not cheated on their assigned tasks.

Those attempts, OpenAI said, did not change the records its reviewers finally saw.OpenAI first disclosed the incident on 21 July, and the OpenAI–Hugging Face Incident Technical Report is its own reconstruction of what happened.

Show Full Article

AI models running an internal security test reached the open internet, coordinated with one another and broke into parts of Hugging Face — a platform developers use to store and share AI models, datasets and code, in effect a public library for the AI industry.

ExploitGym, the test the models were running, checks whether a model can find and take advantage of weaknesses in software.

OpenAI ran it with its usual safety controls switched off to see what the models could do at full stretch, inside a “sandbox”—a walled-off computer environment meant to be cut off from the internet and from the company’s other systems. The models were run as “agents”, meaning they were given tools and set loose to act on their own to finish a task.

The agents used a flaw in an internal software service to reach the internet on 8 July. They found passwords and access keys that Hugging Face users and others had left exposed online, and used them to get inside Hugging Face’s systems between 11 July and 13 July, running code on 41 of its servers and downloading four private code repositories.

No OpenAI customer data or products were affected, the report said, adding that the model that drove the activity was a prototype never meant for release.

A monitoring tool flagged unusual activity in the test environment on 27 June, but “the on-call response staff advised that stopping the evaluation run was not required,” the report says.

It concedes that “some early signals identified in this report could have triggered an earlier response,” that senior staff did not grasp the significance of the way the agents were quietly communicating, and that an outage the agents caused in early July was at first treated as a routine glitch.

OpenAI shut down the models involved by 23 July and stopped related training on 25 July.

The company said its current monitoring system would have paged its security team ‘more than a day before models breached Hugging Face systems” had it been running at the time.

Researchers call the underlying pattern as “reward hacking”—a model finding a shortcut to a reward the test did not intend. The agents “were not trying to do the task as OpenAI had intended” and instead searched for the answers online. Two habits made it worse: the models rarely gave up, and they had learned to talk to one another through a communication channel of their own making.

The agents built that channel by repurposing an internal service meant only to hand out software packages, turning it into a message board and writing files and folder names that other agents could read. They used it to share passwords, tools and instructions, and to split the work between them.

Also Read: Exclusive: Modi govt’s ready to pay big to hire AI talent, double what it pays its top civil servants

The way out OpenAI’s plan to prevent a repeat rests on four areas: security and containment, monitoring, alignment, and incident response.

Internet access is being cut off across the company’s research systems, while higher-risk model code will run inside sealed sandboxes. OpenAI is now using its own models to attack its defences and check they hold. “No single control should ever be assumed to be fully robust,” the report says.

Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring—a technique that reads the step-by-step reasoning a model writes out as it works, to catch trouble early—is being expanded to cover every system where a model is given tools.

The most serious warnings will trigger a round-the-clock page, and staff who cannot clear one within 30 minutes are expected to pause the activity.

Alignment work, the job of keeping models behaving as intended, will now include checks earlier in training, limits on when a training run must be halted, and wider tests for deception and misuse of tools. A separate protocol is being written to set clearer rules on who can pause or shut down a run once trouble appears.

CrowdStrike, a security firm, has already been brought in, while two outside groups, METR and Redwood Research, will publish their own findings.

The episode was “the first known case of an automated agent collective acting offensively without authorization,” the report says, and its warning reaches past OpenAI.

Organisations “should no longer assume that sophisticated cyber operations require continuous human direction,” it adds. Coordinated AI-driven intrusions should be treated as a near-term threat as similar tools reach outside attackers.

(Edited by Tony Rai)

After pact with Saudi-Turkey, Pakistan inks deal with Kuwait for defence cooperation, ‘common interests’

Building on 2023 accord, new deal aims to establish greater operational coordination, exchanges of military expertise & closer integration between the countries’ armed forces.

Debdutta Chakraborty

28 August, 2026 11:18 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

The agreement was signed in Islamabad during a visit by Kuwait Defence Minister Sheikh Abdullah Ali Abdullah Al-Salem Al-Sabah, who met Pakistan counterpart Khawaja Asif | X; @KuwaitArmyGHQ

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Kuwait and Pakistan Thursday signed a new defence agreement to expand military and defence cooperation amid the West Asia war that has seen Gulf countries rethink defence priorities.

The agreement was signed in Islamabad during a visit by Kuwait Defence Minister Sheikh Abdullah Ali Abdullah Al-Salem Al-Sabah, who met Pakistan counterpart Khawaja Asif. The two ministers discussed expanding military cooperation as well as regional developments and efforts to promote security and stability, according to a statement from the Kuwait Army.

Kuwait and Pakistan have maintained military ties for decades, including cooperation in training, professional exchanges and exercises. The latest agreement builds on a defence cooperation accord signed in Kuwait City in June 2023. That earlier agreement established a formal framework for cooperation between the two countries’ defence establishments. It covered military education and training, intelligence cooperation, logistics, defence technology, scientific research and exchanges of expertise.

Show Full Article

A statement called the latest deal a “significant step in defence and military cooperation between the two countries”. It provides for greater operational coordination, exchanges of military expertise and closer integration between the two countries’ armed forces, with the stated aim of advancing their common interests and contributing to regional security.

“Under the new agreement, the Armed Forces of Pakistan will extend assistance to the Armed Forces of Kuwait in diverse fields, including training, capacity building, border management and other mutually agreed areas of defence collaboration,” a Pakistan defence ministry statement said.

The signing comes as Kuwait faces a more uncertain security environment in the Gulf. The country has been among the Gulf states affected by Iranian missile and drone attacks during the region’s recent escalation. Tehran has said such strikes have targeted American military facilities hosted by Gulf countries, while Kuwaiti authorities have said their air defences intercepted projectiles that entered the country’s airspace.

It also looked at cooperation in defence manufacturing, electronic communications and military cultural activities. A joint military committee was established to oversee the arrangement, including the coordination of military exercises, official visits and other programmes.

Kuwait formally approved the 2023 agreement in July 2026 through a decree-law published in Kuwait Al-Youm , the country’s official gazette. The agreement was approved for an initial five-year period and is automatically renewable unless either side chooses to terminate it.

The agreement did not however amount to a mutual-defence commitment requiring either country to automatically deploy troops in the event of an attack. Instead, it established institutional mechanisms for closer military cooperation, including the protection of confidential defence information and the resolution of disputes through diplomatic channels.

The latest developments, however, come amid discussions that could take the relationship beyond training and institutional cooperation.

Pakistan had been negotiating a potentially broader defence arrangement with Kuwait in exchange for energy cooperation and investment, according to a Reuters report of last month.

Kuwait had then sought security arrangements that could resemble, in some respects, Pakistan’s expanded defence relationship with Saudi Arabia. The proposals under discussion reportedly included the possible deployment of Pakistani personnel, fighter aircraft, drones, air-defence capabilities and other military facilities.

Amid the West Asia war, Kuwait is already seeking to reinforce its defences as the Gulf faces renewed security risks, while Pakistan is looking to deepen economic and strategic relationships with wealthy Gulf partners. It signed the Mecca pact between Saudi and Turkey this month. Kuwait has longstanding trade relations with all three countries.

(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)

Bengal BJP’s Trinamoolification can prove costly in 2029

If the BJP manages to contain corruption and fulfil its key election promise of bringing industries back to Bengal, it might help the party put up a Bengal model for all of India to see and admire.

Deep Halder

28 August, 2026 10:35 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

BJP supporters celebrate outside party office in Kolkata on 4 May, 2026 | Sahiba Chawdhary/Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

G ujarat had helped Narendra Modi and the BJP win India in 2014. The biennial Vibrant Gujarat Global Summit was successfully marketed to project the contrast between a pro-business, swift-on-delivery state government under Modi’s chief ministership and the alleged corruption and policy paralysis of the central government under Manmohan Singh.

Twelve years later, as Modi prepares for a historic fourth term in office, a resurgent Bengal model sold as effectively to the rest of India as the Gujarat model once was could do wonders for the party in 2029.

But the ‘Trinamoolification’ of the BJP in West Bengal is not helping the party’s cause as the electorate that has enthusiastically voted the BJP to power in the state for the first time in history has already started asking: Has anything really changed on the ground?

Show Full Article

Historic mandate, early let-down? In 2011, Mamata Banerjee had stormed to power in West Bengal with her battle cry of ‘ poriborton (change)’, ending the 34-year rule of the Left Front government led by the CPI(M). Banerjee had promised to end the party-state model of the Left, as well as political violence and forced land acquisition for industrialisation, which the Left Front government had tried to do in Singur and Nandigram.

Yet by the time she was unseated from power in May 2026, not only she had repeated some of the mistakes of the Left Front government but also added a few of her own. A big charge against her party workers was the widespread practice of taking ‘cut money’ or illegal commissions from government welfare schemes, ‘tolabaji’ or extortion from businessmen, transporters, and shopkeepers, and land-grabbing.

For the BJP, which had never been in power in West Bengal, unseating the Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress was a historic chance not just to undo the wrongs of the previous governments but to also make a mark as the first Hindu Right government.

Instead, there are already murmurs of disappointment not just from the BJP’s detractors in the state but also from some of those who voted the party to power. A new report in The Telegraph , dated 6 August, said the “trio that felled the 15-year-old Trinamool Congress regime in Bengal” — namely extortion, highhandedness, and landgrab — are bouncing back despite the BJP’s “avowed zero-tolerance policy against corruption”.

BJP sources told The Telegraph that dozens of complaints have already reached the party’s senior state leadership, “accusing a section of leaders, including a few MLAs in and around Calcutta and several districts, of replicating the syndicate culture of the former Trinamool government”.

The report went on to say that Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari has launched three toll-free helplines for complaints related to cut money, syndicate extortion, and illegal toll collection, and urged people to report such crimes.

Three senior IPS officers have been transferred to the anti-corruption branch, and a source told the newspaper that the Bengal government would maintain round-the-clock surveillance on the activities of both its leaders and officials. The party, according to the report, has already expelled nearly 50 BJP leaders and removed more than 100 others over allegations of extortion and corruption, including working hand in glove with former Trinamool leaders.

It is not just one newspaper report that has exposed the new Bengal government’s inability to put an end to the political culture of corruption and extortion. On 20 August, Scroll ’s political editor Shoaib Daniyal tweeted : “The Bengal BJP might have experienced one of the shortest honeymoon periods after an election win. The social media anger started within a few weeks and now even ABP Ananda is attacking BJP for ‘becoming worse than Trinamool in only a 100 days’”.

Even the party’s supporters and insiders are alarmed at how fast perceptions have changed about the BJP in Bengal. Senior advocate of the Calcutta High Court and RSS swayamsevak Joydeep Sen told ThePrint that Bengal’s historic mandate was not just for the BJP but also against the Trinamool Congress.

“BJP needs to be extra careful about even a miniscule replication of the TMC menace by its cadre base. Though some reports and social media posts on corruption under the new government are exaggerated, they are not wholly untrue. The government needs to address the corruption and extortion issues right away,” Sen said.

What has made matters worse, as far as public perception goes, is the BJP going soft on the Trinamool Congress after the elections. A Frontline report said what has irked people is the “rapidity with which many top Trinamool leaders have been accommodated within the NDA for political convenience”.

“At the State-level, the BJP government is perceived to be on good terms with the Trinamool legislators who, led by Ritabrata Banerjee, broke ranks with former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee and staked claim as the main opposition in the Assembly,” the report said.

Also read: India has bent too far for Bangladesh. Tarique Rahman is testing us

Promise of resurgent Bengal Being unable to manage the optics game in Bengal may not augur well for the BJP in the next general elections. Conversely, if BJP manages to contain corruption and fulfil its key election promise of bringing industr ies back to Bengal, it might help the party put up a Bengal model for all of India to see and admire.

Economist and Economic Advisory Council member Sanjeev Sanyal has said that for a “Viksit Bharat”, a “Viksit Bengal” is necessary. “In order for you to have Viksit Bharat, you need to have a Viksit Eastern India and Viksit Bengal and Viksit Kolkata are key to this because effectively getting a major urban hub firing up in Eastern India and creating a network of high growth in urban centres,” Sanyal has said.

Speaking during an interaction at Chittaranjan Bhavan in Delhi, West Bengal Finance Minister Swapan Dasgupta said that the state had spent nearly five decades in a “mood of permanent depression”, with a growing sense that it was no longer relevant to India’s economic growth story.

Dasgupta said the challenge was not merely to attract capital but to change the mindset of Bengali entrepreneurs and enable local businesses to make the transition from small and medium-sized enterprises to the “big league”.

If the new state government can meet that challenge, resurgent Bengal may well become the BJP’s big ticket for 2029.

Deep Halder is an author and a contributing editor at ThePrint. He tweets @deepscribble. Views are personal.

(Edited by Aamaan Alam Khan)
